content: In nuclear engineering, a fissile material is defined as a substance capable of sustaining a chain reaction of nuclear fission. All known fissile materials can sustain a chain reaction involving either thermal (slow) neutrons or fast neutrons. This means they can be utilized in various applications, including: Thermal reactors, which require a neutron moderator. Fast reactors, which operate without a neutron moderator. Nuclear explosives. The term fissile is distinct from fissionable. While fissionable refers to any material whose atoms can undergo nuclear fission, fissile specifically describes materials that can undergo fission when interacting with neutrons that have zero kinetic energy. Therefore, all fissile materials are fissionable, but not all fissionable materials are fissile. Some experts even restrict the term fissionable to refer only to non-fissile materials. For example, uranium-238 is fissionable but not fissile. Uranium-235, when interacting with fast neutrons (neutrons with an energy of approximately 1 MeV and a velocity of about 52,000 km/s), can easily induce fission in uranium-238 and other non-fissile actinides. However, the neutrons produced by this fission are not fast enough to sustain a chain reaction in uranium-238, meaning it cannot independently sustain a chain reaction. Fast fission of uranium-238 plays a significant role in the yield and fallout of fission-fusion-fission nuclear weapons. Additionally, fast fission of uranium-238 contributes substantially to the power output of certain fast breeder reactors. Fissile nuclides used in nuclear fuels include: Uranium-235, which is found in natural and enriched uranium. Plutonium-239, which is produced from uranium-238 through neutron capture. Plutonium-241, which is produced from plutonium-240 through neutron capture. Uranium-233, which is produced from thorium-232 through neutron capture. In general, actinide isotopes with an odd number of neutrons are fissile. Most nuclear fuels have an odd number of neutrons (N) and an even number of protons (Z). Isotopes with both an odd number of neutrons and an odd number of protons (odd Z, odd N) are typically short-lived because they undergo beta decay to form isotopes with even numbers of both neutrons and protons (even Z, even N). Fissile nuclides do not have a 100% probability of undergoing fission upon absorbing a neutron. The likelihood of fission depends on the specific nuclide and the energy of the neutron. Fissile materials generally exhibit the following characteristics: A high probability of fission upon neutron capture. The release of two or more neutrons on average per neutron capture, ensuring a sufficient number of neutrons to sustain a chain reaction. A reasonably long half-life. Availability in suitable quantities for practical use. The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) previously categorized fissile materials based on their security requirements for transportation: Fissile Class I: No controls required. Fissile Class II: Limits on the amount of material that can be transported. Fissile Class III: Special shipping arrangements required. These classifications were replaced in the mid-1990s.
